# 2006A Question 2 {.unnumbered}

::: {.exam-question}
## Question {.question-label}

[**What is**]{.task-verb} an isomer? Briefly [**write**]{.task-verb} an account of the types of isomers and their significance in drugs used in anaesthesia.
:::

:::: {#answer-structure}

## Suggested Structure

State what an **Isomer** is, then [**write**]{.task-verb} an account under **Structural Isomers**, **Stereoisomers**, and **Clinical Significance**. Pair examples of anaesthetic drugs with the physicochemical, kinetic or dynamic consequences of their isomerism.

::::

## Examiner Comments

::: {.examiner-comments}
**53 %** of candidates passed this question.

The main points to include were a definition, classification and a description of specific drugs and the implications of isomerism.

Many candidates had incorrect classifications. Some candidates described tautomers as a form of stereoisomers when in fact they are a subtype of structural (or constitutional) isomers. Similarly, a large number of candidates confused geometric isomers with structural isomers. Geometric isomers are stereoisomers that differ in the orientation of groups around a double bond or ring structure. Many of the diagrams were incorrect.

It is also noted that many candidates neglected to mention the clinical significance of isomers. Better answers included specific examples such as enhanced analgesia with S-ketamine, lower cardiotoxicity with levobupivacaine and improved solubility of the enol form of thiopentone.
:::
